title: Marking the Boat to Find the Sword
text:
A man from the state of Chu was crossing a river by boat. Partway across, his sword slipped from its scabbard and fell over the side into the water.

He did not panic. Instead, he took out a knife and carefully cut a notch in the side of the boat, at the exact place where the sword had gone over. That, he said, is where my sword fell.

The boat sailed on and came to land on the far bank. Then the man went to the notch he had made, jumped into the water at that spot, and began searching the riverbed for his sword.

Of course he did not find it. The boat had moved; the sword had not. Looking for it this way, the text remarks, was surely a muddle.

The compilers of the Lushi Chunqiu, writing for the court of Qin in the third century BC, put this story in a chapter arguing that a ruler must examine the present instead of slavishly copying the laws of former kings. Governing a state with the old laws, they wrote, is just like this. The times have moved on, but the laws have not, and to govern that way is very difficult.
lesson: When circumstances change, your reference points change with them. Do not keep searching for answers where they used to be.
source: Lushi Chunqiu, chapter Cha Jin (Examining the Present)
